---
title: "1D model: physical problem"
---

EnerHabitat evaluates the thermal performance of a **single opaque component of the
building envelope** — a wall or a roof. It considers that the only heat path into the
indoor space is through the component under evaluation: there are no windows, no
ventilation, no infiltration and no internal heat gains [@barrios2016]. This makes
results directly comparable
across constructive systems: whatever difference appears in the indoor temperature or in
the energy demand is caused by the constructive system alone.

The simulation runs over the **average day** of a chosen month, built from the EPW weather
file (see [The average day](#the-average-day)), and is iterated day after day until the
solution becomes periodic — the daily cycle repeats itself. All reported results
correspond to that converged, periodic day.

## Domain and assumptions

The constructive system is a stack of $N$ homogeneous layers, ordered from outside
($x = 0$) to inside ($x = L$). Each layer $j$ is described by three constant properties:
thermal conductivity $k_j$ (W/m·K), density $\rho_j$ (kg/m³) and specific heat $c_j$
(J/kg·K).

![1D domain: multilayer wall/roof with its boundary conditions and the indoor-air
node.](img/domain_1d.png){#fig-domain}

The model assumes:

- **1D conduction** perpendicular to the surface (the $x$ direction); layers are
  homogeneous, so there is no in-plane heat flow.
- **Constant thermal properties** per layer (no temperature dependence, no moisture).
- **Convective boundary conditions** with fixed film coefficients $h_o$ (outdoor) and
  $h_i$ (indoor). The defaults, $h_o = 13$ and $h_i = 8.1$ W/m²·K, are the values
  prescribed by the Mexican standards NOM-008-ENER and NOM-020-ENER ($h_i = 8.1$
  is the vertical-surface value, applied here to all orientations); both are
  configurable.
- **Solar and long-wave radiation** on the outdoor surface enter through the sun–air
  temperature (@eq-tsa).
- The indoor space is a **lumped air node** of depth $L_a$ (2.5 m by default) in the
  free-running mode, or a **fixed setpoint** in the air-conditioned mode.

## Governing equations

Within each layer $j$ the temperature field obeys the one-dimensional, time-dependent
heat conduction equation [@incropera2007]:

$$
\rho_j\, c_j\, \frac{\partial T_j}{\partial t} \;=\; k_j\, \frac{\partial^2 T_j}{\partial x^2},
\qquad j = 1, \dots, N,
$$ {#eq-heat}

where $t$ is time and $x$ the coordinate perpendicular to the surface. At the joint
between consecutive layers the temperature is continuous and the conductive flux is
conserved:

$$
k_j \left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right|_{j,\,j+1}
\;=\;
k_{j+1} \left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right|_{j,\,j+1}.
$$ {#eq-continuity}

## Outdoor boundary condition: the sun–air temperature

At the outdoor surface, $x = 0$, convection against the **sun–air temperature** $T_{sa}$
balances the conducted flux:

$$
h_o \left( T_{sa} - T_{x=0} \right)
\;=\;
-\,k_1 \left.\frac{\partial T_1}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0}.
$$ {#eq-bc-out}

$T_{sa}$ is a fictitious temperature that lumps together the three thermal loads on the
exterior surface — convection with outdoor air, absorbed short-wave solar radiation, and
the long-wave radiative exchange with the sky [@ashrae1997]:

$$
T_{sa} \;=\; T_a \;+\; \frac{a\, I_s}{h_o} \;-\; RF,
$$ {#eq-tsa}

where:

- $T_a$ — outdoor air temperature of the average day;
- $I_s$ — solar irradiance on the (tilted, oriented) surface, W/m²;
- $a$ — solar absorptance of the outdoor surface (the *color* of the wall/roof);
- $h_o$ — outdoor film coefficient;
- $RF$ — long-wave radiation factor: EnerHabitat uses $RF = 3.9\ °\mathrm{C}$ for
  horizontal surfaces (`tilt = 0`, a roof facing the cold sky) and $RF = 0$ for any
  other tilt (e.g. vertical walls, `tilt = 90`).

$I_s$ is computed with [pvlib](https://pvlib-python.readthedocs.io/) [@holmgren2018]
from the average-day beam, diffuse and global horizontal irradiances, the solar position
at the site, and the surface `tilt` and `azimuth`. This is why `Tsa()` is recomputed —
automatically, on the next call — whenever the color, the orientation, the month or the
location change.

## Indoor boundary condition and solution modes

At the indoor surface, $x = L$, the conducted flux is released by convection to the
indoor air at temperature $T_i$:

$$
-\,k_N \left.\frac{\partial T_N}{\partial x}\right|_{x=L}
\;=\;
h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_i \right).
$$ {#eq-bc-in}

What happens to $T_i$ defines the two solution modes.

### Free-running mode — `solve()`

The indoor air is a lumped thermal mass — density $\rho_a$, specific heat $c_a$, depth
$L_a$ — whose temperature evolves with the heat received from the indoor surface:

$$
L_a\, \rho_a\, c_a\, \frac{dT_i}{dt} \;=\; h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_i \right),
$$ {#eq-air}

with $L_a = 2.5$ m by default (`config.La`). The air properties are
$\rho_a \approx 1.18$ kg/m³ and $c_a \approx 1005$ J/kg·K (`config.AIR_DENSITY`,
`config.AIR_HEAT_CAPACITY`). Because @eq-air is integrated in time alongside the wall,
the time step is constrained by this coupling — see the
[numerical method](numerics.qmd#indoor-air-coupling-free-running-mode) for why
`config.dt` is fixed at 10 s.

The reported **`energy_transfer`** is the heat delivered by the indoor surface to the
air, accumulated over the converged day:

$$
E \;=\; \int_{24\,\mathrm{h}} h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_i \right)^{+} dt
\qquad \left[\mathrm{J/(m^2\,day)}\right],
$$ {#eq-energy-transfer}

where $(\,\cdot\,)^{+}$ keeps the positive part (heat entering the room). In the
periodic regime the daily energy entering equals the energy leaving, so either one
represents the transfer through the system.

### Air-conditioned mode — `solveAC()`

The indoor air temperature is held constant at the **neutrality temperature** of the
adaptive comfort model of Humphreys & Nicol [-@humphreys2000]:

$$
T_i \;=\; T_n \;=\; 0.54\, \overline{T_a} \;+\; 13.5\ °\mathrm{C},
$$ {#eq-tn}

where $\overline{T_a}$ is the mean outdoor air temperature of the average day. The
cooling and heating demands are the fluxes the air-conditioning system must remove or
supply to keep $T_i = T_n$:

$$
E_c \;=\; \int_{24\,\mathrm{h}} h_i \left( T_{x=L} - T_n \right)^{+} dt,
\qquad
E_h \;=\; \int_{24\,\mathrm{h}} h_i \left( T_n - T_{x=L} \right)^{+} dt,
$$ {#eq-energies-ac}

reported as **`cooling_energy`** and **`heating_energy`** in J/(m²·day).

::: {.callout-note}
The average-day DataFrame also carries **`DeltaTn`**, the half-width of the comfort zone
around $T_n$ as a function of the daily outdoor temperature swing, following the
bioclimatic proposal of Morillón [@morillon2004] (from ±1.25 °C for swings below 13 °C up
to ±3.5 °C for swings above 52 °C). It is provided as data for comfort analyses — e.g.
checking how long the free-running $T_i$ stays inside $T_n \pm \Delta T_n$ — but
`solveAC()` holds the setpoint at $T_n$ itself.
:::

## The average day

The climate forcing is built from the EPW file for the selected month
(`Location.meanDay(month, year)`), at 1-second resolution:

- **Outdoor temperature $T_a$** — the monthly means of the daily minimum and maximum,
  $T_{min}$ and $T_{max}$, are interpolated with the cosine model of Chow & Levermore
  [-@chow2007]: the minimum is assumed at sunrise and the maximum at the month's mean
  time of daily maximum, both extracted from the EPW.
- **Irradiances $I_g$, $I_b$, $I_d$** — the month's hour-by-hour means of global,
  beam and diffuse horizontal irradiance, interpolated in time to the simulation grid.
- **Solar position and sunrise** — computed with pvlib for the site's latitude,
  longitude, altitude and timezone (read from the EPW header).
- **Comfort quantities** — $T_n$ (@eq-tn) and `DeltaTn` (constant columns).

`Tsa()` then evaluates @eq-tsa on this average day for the system's `tilt`, `azimuth`
and `absortance`, and returns it on the same time grid used by the solvers.

## Outputs and units

| Result | Mode | Meaning | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Ti` (`pandas.Series`) | both | Indoor air temperature over the converged day | °C |
| `energy_transfer` | `solve()` | Energy delivered to the indoor air (@eq-energy-transfer) | J/(m²·day) |
| `cooling_energy` | `solveAC()` | Cooling demand to hold $T_n$ (@eq-energies-ac) | J/(m²·day) |
| `heating_energy` | `solveAC()` | Heating demand to hold $T_n$ (@eq-energies-ac) | J/(m²·day) |

Energies are per unit of component surface area, accumulated over one day: divide by
$3600$ for Wh/(m²·day) or by $3.6\times10^6$ for kWh/(m²·day).
